title: Dual-Frequency Key Fobs — One Credential, LF + HF
summary: A dual-frequency key fob packs a 125 kHz LF transponder and a 13.56 MHz HF chip into one 40 × 32 × 6 mm ABS housing. Antenna isolation is verified per unit at < 1 dB cross-coupling. LF options span EM4100, {chip:atmel-t5577:name} and HID Prox emulation; HF spans MIFARE Classic, DESFire EV3 and NTAG. One fob carries users through a 12-24 month LF-to-HF migration in a single issuance event.
heroPoints: One fob, two independent antenna systems — 125 kHz LF (ISO/IEC 18000-2) and 13.56 MHz HF (ISO/IEC 14443-3/-4) — electromagnetically isolated to < 1 dB cross-coupling, verified per unit at production acceptance.
Compact 40 × 32 × 6 mm ABS housing (ultrasonic-welded, IP65 per IEC 60529), only ~1 mm thicker than a single-frequency fob — dual antennas fit without any user-noticeable size penalty.
Migration-bridge credential: users carry the same fob through a 12-24 month LF-to-HF reader rollout with zero second-issuance event and zero mid-migration access interruption.

sections.title: One credential, two frequencies
sections.intro: One fob, two frequencies — and no re-badging the building. A 125 kHz LF transponder and a 13.56 MHz HF chip share a single 40 × 32 × 6 mm ABS housing, so one credential carries a site from its Wiegand past into its OSDP future and staff get issued once instead of twice.
bullets: Two independent antenna systems, electromagnetically isolated to < 1 dB cross-coupling and verified per unit at production acceptance.
LF options span EM4100, T5577 and HID Prox emulation; HF spans MIFARE Classic, DESFire EV3 and NTAG.
A single issuance event spans the full 12-24 month LF-to-HF migration — no second re-badging and no mid-migration access interruption.

image.alt: Cutaway of one ABS key-fob housing showing a planar 13.56 MHz HF coil on the outer loop and a heavier-wound 125 kHz LF coil on the inner ring, orthogonally routed to under 1 dB cross-coupling.

sections.title: Why the two chips don't fight
sections.intro: Two orders of magnitude apart in frequency, the two chips never notice each other. A planar HF coil forms the outer loop and a heavier-wound LF coil sits on the inner ring, routed orthogonally, so the two antennas are electromagnetically isolated with no mutual interference — the LF reader energises only the LF coil, the HF reader only the HF coil. Cross-coupling sensitivity degradation stays under < 1 dB, verified per unit on a both-frequency test rig.
bullets: LF coil: heavier multi-turn copper winding on the inner ring for the ISO/IEC 18000-2 inductive envelope.
HF coil: planar coil forming the outer loop for the ISO/IEC 14443-3 / NFC Forum Type 2-4 envelope; orthogonal routing avoids mutual-inductance crosstalk.
When presented to a 125 kHz reader, only the LF chip energises and responds. When presented to a 13.56 MHz reader, only the HF chip energises and responds.
Production acceptance rejects any unit where cross-coupling affects sensitivity by more than 1 dB against a single-chip baseline — per-unit test, both frequencies.

image.alt: A 125 kHz LF reader energises only the LF coil and a 13.56 MHz HF reader only the HF coil in the same fob, with under 1 dB cross-coupling and no mutual interference.

sections.title: Spans both reader eras
sections.intro: The credential outlives the wiring debate. A dual-frequency fob answers to whatever the panel behind the reader speaks — the incumbent Wiegand fleet today, the modernised OSDP link tomorrow — so the reader-to-panel retrofit can proceed on its own schedule, independent of the credential already in the user's pocket.

sections.title: Single-frequency vs dual-frequency — the migration question
sections.intro: The decision hinges on whether the site will carry two reader generations in parallel for an extended period. If the fleet is LF-only or HF-only on day one and will remain so for the life of the fob, single-frequency is cheaper. If the fleet will be mixed for 12+ months, dual-frequency pays back before the migration closes because it removes the second re-issuance event.

sections.title: Quantified case for dual-frequency during migration windows

dataHighlight.heading: Help-desk ticket reduction and procurement-SKU cost saving from field deployments
dataHighlight.text: Property-management reference running 800 tenants across 15 buildings with mixed reader generations recorded a 65 % reduction in credential-related help-desk tickets within 90 days of switching from dual-single-frequency issuance to a single dual-frequency fob. A separate logistics operator with parking (EM4100) and warehouse (MIFARE Classic) access reduced procurement SKUs from two to one and cut credential inventory cost by 22 %. The pattern holds when the mixed-reader window exceeds 9-12 months — below that, single-frequency still wins on unit economics. Above 9-12 months, dual-frequency pays back on help-desk overhead alone before the migration closes.
dataHighlight.source: Proud Tek integration-audit benchmarks (2022-2026) across 9 multi-building-campus + property-management + logistics customers with paired pre- and post-dual-frequency ticket telemetry.

sections.title: Dual-frequency migration timeline — standard 12-24 month enterprise pattern
sections.intro: The single-re-issuance-event enterprise migration runs through three operational phases. Proud Tek's chip-pair preset ({chip:atmel-t5577:name} LF + DESFire EV3 HF) covers the full envelope; faster or slower rollouts simply scale the phase-2 duration.

items.label: Month 0 · Single re-issuance event — dual-frequency fob distribution
items.text: All staff / tenants receive a dual-frequency fob in one issuance event. Both chips are pre-encoded (LF with existing facility code + card number, HF with new AES-128 application keys per NXP AN10922 diversification). Access continues uninterrupted because the LF half still opens every reader; the HF half is dormant until HF readers go live.

items.label: Month 1-3 · Pilot building HF reader install + OSDP v2.2 reader-to-panel retrofit
items.text: One building or one floor receives new HF readers. Reader-to-panel wiring is simultaneously upgraded from legacy Wiegand 5-wire to SIA OSDP v2.2 RS-485 Secure Channel. Dual-frequency fobs authenticate via HF AES-128 against the new readers while the rest of the campus continues on LF — no credential change.

items.label: Month 3-18 · Rolling HF reader rollout building by building
items.text: HF readers are deployed one building or one zone at a time. Because every user already carries a dual-frequency fob, the rollout never blocks on credential availability — the integrator schedules purely around electrician / network capacity. This is the bulk of the migration window and has zero user-facing disruption.

items.label: Month 18-24 · HF coverage reaches 100 % — LF readers retired
items.text: The last LF reader comes offline. The LF half of the dual-frequency fob is no longer authoritative — only the HF AES-128 authentication grants access. The LF chip remains physically present in the fob but inactive; no credential reissue is required and the signed UID-correlation file remains the reconciliation record in the ACS.

items.label: Month 24+ · Steady-state HF-only operation
items.text: Programme experience across system-migration, multi-building-campus, parking-plus-office, mixed-tenant-portfolio and LF-to-HF-bridge dual-frequency-keyfob contributes the audit, refresh and onboarding patterns that inform this solution's operating playbook. the site operates on HF AES-128 only, the dual-frequency fobs in circulation act as single-frequency HF fobs for the remainder of their service life, and the next natural re-issuance happens organically at fob end-of-life (5-10 years) rather than as a migration event.

faq.question: Is the fob bigger than a standard single-frequency fob?
faq.answer: Only slightly. Our dual-frequency fob is 40×32×6 mm — about 1 mm thicker than a standard single-frequency fob. The size difference is imperceptible on a keychain. The dual antenna design fits within the standard fob form factor through careful coil positioning.

faq.question: Can you match our existing fobs?
faq.answer: Yes. Send us samples of both your LF and HF fobs (or tell us the reader models) and we produce a single dual-frequency fob that matches both. We provide a UID correlation table linking the LF and HF chip IDs for each fob.

faq.question: How do I program both chips?
faq.answer: Each chip is programmed independently using its respective frequency reader/writer. We can pre-encode both chips at our factory. Provide your LF credentials (facility code, card number) and HF credentials (sector keys, access data) and we program everything before shipment. A UID mapping file is included with each order.

faq.question: Does the LF chip interfere with the HF chip during a dual-frequency scan?
faq.answer: No. The two antennas are tuned to very different frequencies (125 kHz and 13.56 MHz — two orders of magnitude apart) and the coil geometries are designed for electromagnetic isolation. Each chip only responds to its own band; a 125 kHz reader energises only the LF coil and a 13.56 MHz reader energises only the HF coil. Proud Tek verifies isolation per unit during production by running both chips against a test reader of each frequency and rejecting any unit where cross-coupling affects sensitivity by more than 1 dB.

faq.question: What's the typical migration timeline with dual-frequency fobs?
faq.answer: A typical enterprise LF-to-HF migration runs 12-18 months. Phase 1: issue dual-frequency fobs to all users in a single re-issuance event (zero access disruption because both chips work). Phase 2: roll out new HF readers building by building over 6-12 months. Phase 3: firmware-cut-over to disable LF mode on the dual-frequency credential (or simply retire the LF reader fleet) and operate HF-only. Because users carry the same fob throughout, there is no second issuance event and no mid-migration access interruption — this is the pattern Proud Tek's logistics-operator and corporate-campus references ran through.
